title: Turk Site, Carlisle County
summary: In Carlisle County, the Turk Site was a small but planned Mississippian town with mounds around a plaza, occupied mainly from about AD 1100 to 1300.
bodyMarkdown:
The Turk Site, recorded as 15Ce6, sits on a bluff spur near Bardwell in Carlisle County, overlooking the floodplain of the Mississippi River. According to the [Kentucky Heritage Council's survey of the Mississippi period](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Learn-More/Documents/Mississippi%20Period%20Chapter%20The%20Archaeology%20of%20Kentucky%20An%20update%20Volume%202.pdf), the town covered about 2.5 hectares. It was small, but it was a planned town with mounds arranged around a plaza.

## A town on the bluffs

Turk was home to a Mississippian farming community. The Heritage Council chapter dates its main occupation to the Dorena phase, about A.D. 1100–1300. People continued to live there into the early part of the Medley phase, which runs from about 1300 to 1500.

Turk did not stand alone. The Marshall Site (15Ce27) lies on the next bluff spur, and the chapter suggests that the community's main settlement shifted a few hundred meters south from Marshall to Turk during the Dorena phase.

## The mounds and the plaza

[The Turk Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turk_Site) describes the classic Mississippian layout of mounds facing an open plaza. Several smaller outer mounds were noted by observers in the late 1800s, but they have since been destroyed.

The site has a long record of study. Robert Loughridge described it in 1888. In 1916 Clarence B. Moore dug a pit into Mound C. In the 1980s Richard Edging of the University of Illinois carried out the key modern work and published his results in 1985 and 1990.

## Daily life at Turk

Edging's excavations found a midden, or trash deposit, 0.5 to 1 meter deep. Beneath it were wall-trench house foundations, storage pits and fire basins. Infant burials were found within the settlement.

The town's food came from both fields and forest. The Heritage Council chapter lists maize along with deer, raccoon and turkey. That mix of farming and hunting fed Mississippian towns all along the central Mississippi Valley. Communities in this region were part of a wider [Mississippian culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture) of mound centers that stretched across much of the Southeast and Midwest.

## Neighbors on the river

Turk was one of several mound towns in far western Kentucky. Downriver near the mouth of the Ohio, the people of [Wickliffe Mounds](/stories/wickliffe-mounds-mississippian-village-ballard-county/) built a larger town in roughly the same centuries. The [Adams Site](/stories/adams-site-15fu4/) in Fulton County and the [Rowlandton Mound](/stories/rowlandton-mound-site-15mcn3-paducah/) near Paducah add to the picture of a busy, connected river world.

## Kentucky today

The Turk Site is not developed as a public park. Its value lies in what Edging's work recorded about a small Mississippian town on the bluffs. The nearest place where visitors can see a Mississippian town interpreted on site is Wickliffe Mounds State Historic Site in Ballard County.
